strengths: The paper proposes a simple and effective idea: using panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface so that pretrained 2D VLMs can be reused for 3D visual grounding. This is practically attractive because it preserves 360-degree scene context and avoids the limited field of view of perspective-image VLM pipelines.

The method is a complete and well-engineered pipeline: structure-aware camera placement, multi-modal panoramic rendering, a lightweight adapter for injecting geometric and semantic features into a VLM, visibility-aware 3D aggregation, an EMD loss for numeric supervision, and auxiliary geometric QA training.

Experiments are extensive and largely convincing. PanoGrounder achieves state-of-the-art or top-2 results on ScanRefer, Nr3D, and Sr3D, with particularly strong gains on human-written Nr3D queries, and further shows zero-shot promise, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to text perturbations.

The ablations are broad: input modalities, EMD loss, geometric QA, camera placement factors, number of cameras, adapter layer placement, scene representations, test-time augmentation, and per-category/elevation analysis. This gives useful insight into which components matter.
Qualitative results and failure-case analyses are included, and the paper honestly discusses limitations such as reconstruction dependence, inference speed, and restricted query types.

Clarity is generally good. The main paper describes the pipeline clearly, and the supplementary material provides substantial implementation details, prompt templates, hyperparameters, and additional analyses, which improves reproducibility.

The work is potentially impactful for robotics, AR, and embodied AI because it suggests a practical way to leverage modern VLMs for 3D grounding without designing task-specific 3D tokens or training 3D encoders from scratch.
The deployment experiment on a self-captured scene, while limited, is a useful step toward demonstrating practical viability beyond clean benchmark meshes.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is limited. The core idea of using panoramas to bridge 2D VLMs and 3D grounding is intuitive, and the method relies heavily on off-the-shelf components such as CogVLM, SAM, DINOv2, Mask3D, RANSAC, PyTorch3D, and ODGS. The contribution is more a well-executed system/pipeline than a fundamentally new formulation.

The method depends strongly on high-quality 3D reconstruction. Main results use mesh-rendered panoramas or cleaned 3D scenes, while fully automated reconstruction (3DGS*) drops to 55.1 from 61.6 and excludes many ScanNet scenes because COLMAP fails to register enough images. This weakens the claim that the approach relaxes 3D input requirements and is broadly practical.

Several evaluations use oracle-like 3D information. Generalization experiments use GT object masks, the ReferIt3D two-stage variant relies on GT candidate point cloud segments, and some ablations use GT segmentation. These choices isolate 2D grounding performance but are not fully end-to-end 3D visual grounding and may favor the method relative to point-cloud baselines.

Fairness of comparison is not fully controlled. Baselines differ in input representation (point clouds vs. rendered meshes/panoramas), training data (single-dataset vs. multi-dataset), and backbone capacity. Some baseline results are re-run by the authors, while others are cited; this makes it difficult to attribute gains purely to the proposed representation.

The computational cost is substantial. Offline per-scene processing includes COLMAP (~87 min), 3DGS training (~43 min), semantic feature lifting (~24 min), and rendering, while online inference uses a 17B VLM at ~3.3s per query and ~51.6 GB GPU memory. This is heavy for real-time robotics or large-scale deployment, and the efficiency analysis covers only a single self-captured scene.

Some component gains are modest or mixed. EMD, geometric feature injection, geometric QA, and adapter layer placement produce small improvements (e.g., adapter placement varies only between 60.9 and 61.0), and the paper does not report variance across seeds or statistical significance. More rigorous disentangling of contributions would strengthen the empirical case.

The panoramic representation has inherent limitations: equirectangular distortion, a floor-based grid that assumes a single indoor floor plane, limited vertical field of view, and no evaluation on outdoor, multi-floor, or dynamic scenes. The authors acknowledge some of these, but they remain important open issues for the claimed generalizability.

The text-generalization experiments use LLaMA-generated paraphrases and affordance variants. While the trend is interesting, especially on +Aff.-N, the mechanism behind the large relative improvement is not deeply analyzed, and generated text may not reflect real user language distributions.

The paper does not release code or checkpoints in the main text, and reproducibility details such as random seeds and training variance are missing. Although the supplementary material is helpful, full reproduction of the 17B-VLM and reconstruction pipeline remains non-trivial.

The state-of-the-art claim should be qualified. Because different methods use different input assumptions, backbones, and training protocols, the reported improvements establish strong performance on the chosen benchmarks but not necessarily dominance across the full 3DVG design space.
